lesson.title: Scaling Past select(): epoll and kqueue
lesson.summary: epoll on Linux and kqueue on BSD and macOS solve the same readiness-notification problem as select() and poll(), but by having the kernel remember what it is watching, they avoid re-scanning every socket on every call.
lesson.body:
The core inefficiency in select() and poll() is that the caller has to describe its entire set of watched sockets fresh on every call, and the kernel has to re-walk that whole set to figure out what changed. epoll on Linux and kqueue on the BSD family, including macOS, fix this by flipping the model. Instead of handing the kernel a full list every time, a program registers its sockets once, up front, and the kernel keeps a persistent record of what it is watching. From then on, the program simply asks what has become ready since it last checked, and the kernel only has to hand back the sockets that actually changed state, rather than re-checking every socket in the set from scratch.

On Linux, this looks like three separate steps. epoll_create() makes a kernel-side epoll instance, epoll_ctl() adds, modifies, or removes individual sockets from that instance's interest list, and epoll_wait() blocks until at least one watched socket is ready and returns just those. Because the kernel already tracks which sockets belong to the interest list and updates their status as events happen, instead of being asked to re-derive that status on every call, the cost of epoll_wait() scales with the number of sockets that are actually active, not the total number being watched. A server holding ten thousand mostly idle connections, where only a handful have new data at any given moment, pays for those few active sockets, not all ten thousand.

kqueue, found on BSD systems and macOS, solves the same problem through a somewhat different interface. A single kqueue() call creates the kernel event queue, and kevent() is used both to register or change interest and to retrieve ready events, all through one call. Conceptually it plays the same role as epoll, persistent kernel-side tracking so a program is not restating its whole interest set every time it waits, and it is also notably more general than epoll, since kqueue can report on more than just socket readiness, including file changes, process events, and timers, depending on the platform.

epoll adds one more distinction worth knowing. It can operate in level-triggered mode, the default, where it keeps reporting a socket as ready as long as unread data remains, matching the intuitive behavior of select() and poll(), or in edge-triggered mode, where it only reports a socket the moment its state changes, and the program is expected to keep reading, or writing, until it gets an EWOULDBLOCK or EAGAIN, or risk missing that more data was actually still there. Edge-triggered mode can reduce the number of wakeups under heavy load, but it demands more careful code, since a program that stops reading after only draining part of a buffer will not be reminded there is more.

The upshot is that epoll and kqueue are what actually let modern servers, web servers, proxies, and event-driven frameworks alike hold open hundreds of thousands of connections on a single thread or a small pool of threads, something that was simply not practical with select() or poll() once connection counts grew large. They are also more complex to use correctly than select() and poll(), which is why the simpler tools still see plenty of use in smaller-scale programs.
